pages.title: How is a GPU different from a CPU?
claims: CPUs optimize for a few, fast threads while GPUs optimize for many many threads
Many tiny compute units (ALUs).
CPUs optimize for latency (each thread finishes quickly)
Much less support for branching (control, cache)
GPUs optimize for throughput (total processed data)

pages.title: Anatomy of a GPU (execution units)
claims: Each SM further contains many SPs
GPUs have many SM (streaming
(streaming processor) that can
multiprocessors) that independently
execute ‘threads’ in parallel
execute ‘blocks’ (jobs).

pages.title: Anatomy of a GPU (memory)
claims: The closer the memory to the SM, the faster it is – L1 and shared memory is inside
the SM. L2 cache is on die, and global memory are the memory chips next to the GPU
SRAM (shared/cache memory) is much more expensive (100x) but ~ 8x faster than DRAM (Global memory)

pages.title: Execution model of a GPU
claims: There are 3 important players in the execution model
Threads: Threads ‘do the work’ in parallel – all threads execute the same instructions but with
different inputs (SIMT).
Blocks: Blocks are groups of threads. Each block runs on a SM w/ its own shared memory.
Warp: Threads always execute in a ‘warp’ of 32 consecutively numbered threads each.

pages.title: Memory model of a GPU
claims: Each thread can access its own register, and shared memory within the block.
Information that goes across blocks need to be read/written to global memory (slow)

Differences - how the accelerators are networked (in the parallelism lecture)
no warps (just blocks – tradeoffs in matmul vs non-matmul)

pages.title: How do we make GPUs go fast?
claims: 1. Control divergence (not a memory bottleneck..)
2. Low precision computation
3. Operator fusion
4. Recomputation
5. Coalescing memory
6. Tiling

pages.title: Control divergence (not a memory issue)
claims: GPUs operate in a SIMT model – every thread in a warp is executing the same instruction
Conditionals are fine, but lead to significant overhead from the execution model

pages.title: Trick 1: Low precision computation
claims: If you have fewer bits, you have fewer bits to move

pages.title: Low precision improves arithmetic intensity
claims: Example: elementwise ReLU (𝑥 = max(0, 𝑥)) on a vector of size 𝑛.
(Float 32 case)
Memory access: 1 read (x), 1 write (if x < 0), float 32 = 4 bytes per op
Operations: 1 comparison op, 1 FLOP.
Intensity: 8 bytes / FLOP
(Float 16)
Memory access: 1 read (x), 1 write (if x < 0), float 16 = 2 bytes per op
Operations: 1 comparison op, 1 FLOP.
Intensity: 4 bytes / FLOP

pages.title: Low precision drives faster matrix multiplies
claims: Lots of operations in modern GPUs are accelerated via low / mixed precision operations
Tensor cores

pages.title: Frontiers in low precision
claims: Very low precision (FP8) with different tradeoffs
Multiple scaling factors MXFP8 (Blackwell)
MXFP8 has many interesting things about it
Uses E4M3 (more mantissa) due to more scale factors
Scale factors themselves are FP8 (E8M0), 1 per 32
Transposes are now nontrivial!

pages.title: MXFP8 training in practice
claims: Notice – not all weights in MXFP8, transposes also separately quantized

pages.title: Frontiers in low precision
claims: MXFP4..
This is all the values you can represent! 1 per 16 scaling, E4M3 scaling factors.

pages.title: Trick 2: Operator fusion
claims: Think of a GPU like a factory – inputs come from a warehouse (memory) and is
processed at a factory
Compute scales up, memory doesn’t

pages.title: Operator fusion to minimize memory access
claims: What if we have to do many operations? Shipping back and forth is somewhat silly
Naïve (non-fused)
Fused kernel

pages.title: Example – sines and cosines
claims: Computing sin 2 𝑥 + cos 2 𝑥 naively launches 5 CUDA kernels (back and forth)

pages.title: Fusion example
claims: All 5 pointwise operations can be fused into a single CUDA kernel call.
‘Easy’ fusions like this can be done automatically by compilers (torch.compile)

pages.title: Trick 3: recomputation
claims: In backpropagation, we store the activations (yellow) and compute Jacobians (green)

pages.title: Storing (and retrieving) activations can be expensive!
claims: Let’s say we stack 3 sigmoids on top of each other.
This is really terrible for perf – 8 mem read/writes, very low arithmetic intensity.

pages.title: Throw away the activations, re-compute them!
claims: Throwing away computation can actually be optimal, w/ 5/8 th the memory accesses!

pages.title: Trick (?) 4: Memory coalescing and DRAM
claims: DRAM (global memory) is read in ‘burst mode’ – each read gives you many bytes!
 Burst mode comes from the slow per-row copy to the sense amplifier

pages.title: Memory coalescing
claims: Memory accesses are coalesced if all the threads (in a warp) fall within the same burst
Reminder: a warp is a set of 32 consecutively
numbered threads that execute together in a
block. Memory accesses happen together

pages.title: Coalescing for matrix multiplication
claims: For row-major matrices – threads that move along rows are not coalesced
figures_mentioned: Note how the second diagram reads the entire vector at each step!

pages.title: Trick 5 (the big one): tiling
claims: Tiling is the idea of grouping and ordering threads to minimize global memory access.
Let’s go back to matrix multiplication..
Note that memory access is not coalesced, and repeated (M0,0 and N1,0)

pages.title: Tiling – store and reuse information in shared memory
claims: Cut up the matrix into smaller ‘tiles’, and load this into shared memory
Compute the matrix multiply in ‘phases’
1. Load 𝑀0,0 and 𝑁0,0 tiles into SHM
2. Compute partial sums for 𝑃
(Done with one tile)
3. Load the 𝑀0,0 and 𝑁2,0 tile into SHM
Advantages: repeated reads now access shared, not global memory
and memory access can be coalesced

pages.title: Tiling math
claims: Non-tiled matrix multiply: each input is read 𝑁 times from global memory
Tiled matrix multiply: each input is read times from global memory, and 𝑇 times
within each tile. This is a factor of 𝑇 reduction in global memory access

pages.title: Complexities with tiling
claims: Tile sizes may not divide the matrix size and lead to low utilization
Factors affecting tile sizes
Coalesced memory access
Shared memory size
Divisibility of the matrix dim

pages.title: Complexities with tiling 2 – memory alignment
claims: Memory comes in bursts
Loading tiles are fast if
bursts align with the matrix
Coalesced accesses may be impossible depending on the dimension of the matrix..
(have to do padding)
